chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad ibn Isa or Ibn Abi Umayr, from Ibn Udhaynah, from Zurarah, who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): A man wrote the divorce of his wife or the manumission of his slave, then changed his mind and erased it. He said: 'That is not a divorce nor a manumission until he speaks it.'

key_terms.بَدَا لَهُ: Changed his mind / It became apparent to him

ai.seo_question: Is a written divorce or manumission effective if erased before verbal declaration?
ai.summary: In this narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS), the concept of *al-ibrah bi-l-qawl* (reliance on speech) is applied to written deeds, establishing that mere inscription does not finalize the legal act of *talaq* or *itq* if the author revokes it before verbalizing it. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential emphasis on the intention (*niyyah*) coupled with the vocal expression as the definitive moment of legal effect, distinguishing it from the Hanafi view which often considers writing sufficient. It underscores the principle that written words are merely evidence until they are articulated, ensuring clarity in family law transactions.
